title: The Frankfurt School
keyWorks: T. Adorno and M. Horkheimer, Dialectic of Enlightenment (1947)
E. Fromm, The Art of Loving (1956)
E. Fromm, To Have or to Be? (1976)
summary: The Frankfurt School was a circle of philosophers and sociologists who, from the 1920s on, worked around the Institute for Social Research in Frankfurt. They combined philosophy, sociology and psychoanalysis to understand how the structure of society shapes a person’s inner life. Erich Fromm, Theodor Adorno, Max Horkheimer and Herbert Marcuse asked, in different ways but with equal persistence: why, in a society of abundance, do people so often feel unfree and unhappy?
onEmotions: For the Frankfurt School, feelings are not only a private matter: they reflect the society we live in. Fromm spoke of “social character” — the typical traits a society cultivates in people so that they fit into it well. Adorno and Marcuse showed how the culture of entertainment and consumption shapes our desires and even our idea of freedom. From this follows an important and often relieving thought: your anxiety, fatigue or emptiness is not necessarily just your personal failure. To understand the social causes of a feeling is to stop blaming yourself for it and to hear in it the voice of a living person.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is an understandable reaction, especially in a world where so much is unstable. In Escape from Freedom (1941), Erich Fromm showed that modern people have been released from old ties — estate, community, rigid traditions — and gained “freedom from.” But with it came loneliness and insecurity: now everything depends on you, and there seems to be nothing to lean on. Fromm described how people try to escape this anxiety — by submitting to authority or dissolving into the crowd (“automaton conformity”). In To Have or to Be? he added: if a person defines themselves by what they have — money, status, relationships — they will inevitably be anxious, since all of it can be lost. Fromm saw the way out not in new armor but in “freedom to”: in living engagement, love, creativity. Your anxiety is not a defect; in part, it is the price of freedom.
anxiety.practice: Notice which of the things you are anxious about right now belong to “having” (what can be lost) and which to “being” (who you are and what you do).

quote.text: If I am what I have and if what I have is lost, who then am I?
quote.author: Erich Fromm

fear.text: Fear is one of the most ancient human experiences, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. Adorno and Horkheimer open Dialectic of Enlightenment (1947) with the idea that reason and science sought from the very beginning to free people from fear of nature. But their conclusion is unsettling: a society built on control over nature and people gives rise to new fears — of an impersonal system, of turning out to be “superfluous.” Fromm, in Escape from Freedom, said that many people fear freedom itself and are ready to give it up for a sense of security. From this point of view, your fear is not just an inner problem: it often responds to the real fragility of life in the modern world. Acknowledging this means you can stop thinking of yourself as “too sensitive” and see that many people fear the same thing.
fear.practice: Ask yourself: “Is this fear only mine, or is it shared by many people around me?” Sometimes this question alone makes it a little lighter.

sadness.text: Sadness is not a glitch in your mood but an honest response to what is happening. In One-Dimensional Man (1964), Herbert Marcuse described the “happy consciousness” — an attitude in which consumer society invites us to be content and not ask unnecessary questions. In such a world, sadness is easily mistaken for a malfunction to be fixed as quickly as possible. Marcuse, on the contrary, valued “the power of negative thinking” — the ability to see that reality could be different and better. Adorno went even further: for him, letting suffering speak is a condition of all truth. From this point of view, your sadness may be a form of clarity: you are noticing what not everyone wants to notice. It doesn’t need to be urgently replaced with positivity — it can be given a voice.
sadness.practice: Write, without softening it: “I’m sad because…” — and leave the sentence without a comforting conclusion.

quote.text: The need to lend a voice to suffering is a condition of all truth.
quote.author: Theodor Adorno

grief.text: Grief is a deep and legitimate feeling, and it has no correct timeline. In To Have or to Be?, Erich Fromm distinguished two modes of existence. In the “having” mode we treat people and things as possessions; in the “being” mode, as a living relationship in which we ourselves take part. From Fromm’s point of view, one might say that what has been lost is not something you “had” but something you lived by — which is why the pain is so great. But everything lived in the mode of being — love, attention, shared moments — has become part of who you are and cannot simply be taken away. In Eros and Civilization, Marcuse wrote of memory as a force that preserves the experience of happiness once lived. To remember is not to be stuck; it is a way of going on loving.
grief.practice: Write down one thing you learned alongside the person or thing you have lost. That is what has stayed with you.

loneliness.text: Loneliness is one of the most painful feelings, and it is broader than it seems. In The Art of Loving (1956), Erich Fromm wrote that the awareness of our separateness from others is the deepest source of human anxiety, and the need to overcome that separateness is the deepest human need. He described false ways of escaping loneliness: dissolving into a group, living “like everyone else,” filling time with consumption. Such conformity gives a sense of belonging, but not real closeness. The true answer, for Fromm, is love as an active relationship in which two people unite while remaining themselves. And one more relieving thought from the school: loneliness is largely produced by a society in which relationships increasingly become exchanges. Your feeling is not a verdict on you but a longing for living connection.
loneliness.practice: Think about whom you recently had a conversation with that was brief, perhaps, but alive and not “transactional.” What made it alive?

anger.text: Anger is a normal feeling, and sometimes there is truth in it. In The Anatomy of Human Destructiveness (1973), Erich Fromm distinguished two kinds of aggression. “Benign,” defensive aggression serves life: it arises when your boundaries, dignity or freedom are threatened. “Malignant” aggression is destructive; it grows out of powerlessness and alienation. Marcuse spoke of the “Great Refusal” — the capacity to say “no” to what makes life poorer. From this point of view, your anger may be a signal: something is constraining you or others, and you feel it. What matters is not to suppress it or turn it against yourself, but to understand what exactly it is protecting — and to find a form for that which harms neither you nor anyone else.
anger.practice: Finish the sentence: “My anger is protecting…” — and see what value stands behind it.

shame.text: Shame is a heavy feeling, and it often arrives uninvited. Fromm described the “marketing orientation” — a type of character cultivated by a society in which everything is for sale. A person begins to perceive themselves as a commodity: what matters is not who they are but how well they “sell” — how attractive, successful, in demand they are. Hence a distinctly modern shame: as if you were not “competitive” enough as a person. In Minima Moralia (1951), Adorno showed how the pressure of society penetrates the most private corners of life. From this point of view, part of your shame may not be personal guilt but a consequence of yardsticks imposed on everyone. You can ask yourself: on whose scale am I grading myself right now?
shame.practice: Write down what “standard” you feel you are failing to meet. Who set it — you yourself, or the world around you?

guilt.text: Guilt can be justified, and it can be out of all proportion. In Man for Himself (1947), Erich Fromm distinguished two kinds of conscience. The “authoritarian conscience” is the internalized voice of an external authority — parents, bosses, society; it makes us feel guilty for disobedience. The “humanistic conscience” is our own voice, calling us to our own growth and to fullness of life. Adorno added a bitter but liberating thought: in an unjustly ordered world it is impossible to live a perfectly “right” life. So part of your guilt is not a personal failure but a consequence of the fact that flawlessness is unattainable in principle. This doesn’t cancel responsibility for specific actions, but it lets you tell it apart from endless self-accusation.
guilt.practice: Ask yourself: whose voice speaks in my guilt — my own, or someone else’s, familiar from long ago?

quote.text: Wrong life cannot be lived rightly.
quote.author: Theodor Adorno

envy.text: Everyone knows envy, especially in a world where other people’s success is constantly on display. In One-Dimensional Man, Marcuse distinguished “true” from “false” needs. False needs are those imposed from outside and sustained by advertising and consumer culture: wanting what others have, looking and living the same way. Fromm spoke of the “having” mode, in which a person’s worth is measured by what they possess, and comparison becomes endless. From this point of view, envy is often fed not by your real desires but by a system that constantly shows you what you don’t have. This doesn’t make you a petty person. But you can ask: do I really want this — or was I taught to want it?
envy.practice: Think about the object of your envy and ask: “If no one ever found out I had it, would I still want it?”

emptiness.text: Emptiness is an oppressive state, and it doesn’t mean something is wrong with you. Fromm wrote about “alienation”: a person in modern society may feel not like the author of their life but like a cog in it, playing roles written by others. They do what is required, buy what they are supposed to, but don’t experience themselves as the living source of their own actions. Hence an emptiness that new things don’t fill. Marcuse showed that a society of abundance can satisfy many needs and still leave people unfree. Against this Fromm set the “productive orientation” — a life in which you yourself create, love, think. From this point of view, emptiness is not the absence of you but a sign that the living part of you wants more than consumption.
emptiness.practice: Recall a moment when you were making something yourself — cooking, writing, fixing, helping. What did you feel then?

confusion.text: Confusion is natural: the world is complex, and there are fewer and fewer ready-made answers. Fromm saw this as the flip side of freedom. When external authorities and traditions stop telling people how to live, they gain room to move — and at the same time lose their footing. In Escape from Freedom Fromm showed how tempting it is at such moments to grab hold of someone who will tell you what to think, or simply do “what everyone does.” But he believed another path was possible — “freedom to”: a gradual, independent discovery of what you value. For Fromm, life is a continual birth of oneself, and it is never clear from the first step. From this point of view, confusion is not a failure but a place where this slow process can begin.
confusion.practice: Instead of asking “what should I do?”, ask yourself something else for a minute: “what truly matters to me right now?”

fatigue.text: Fatigue and burnout are not a personal weakness but often the predictable result of a way of life. In Eros and Civilization (1955), Herbert Marcuse introduced the concept of the “performance principle”: in modern society a person’s worth is measured by their efficiency. He also spoke of “surplus repression” — restrictions not needed for survival that serve to maintain a particular order of work and consumption. In his essay “Free Time” (1969), Adorno observed that even rest is often organized as a continuation of work: it has to be “spent productively.” From this point of view, your burnout says not that you aren’t trying hard enough but that the demands exceed human measure. Rest is not a reward for merit; it is your right.
fatigue.practice: Set aside five minutes today that don’t need to be “filled productively” with anything. Just notice how hard or easy that is.

boredom.text: Boredom can be agonizing, even when entertainment is everywhere. Adorno and Horkheimer introduced the concept of the “culture industry”: entertainment is produced as a standardized commodity, and leisure comes to resemble work — just as monotonous and predictable. In his essay “Free Time,” Adorno linked boredom to unfreedom: when a person can’t truly dispose of themselves, their free time doesn’t become free. Marcuse described “one-dimensionality” — a life in which everything is offered in advance and there is no room for anything else. From this point of view, boredom is not your inability to enjoy yourself but, perhaps, a reaction to a world that is too uniform. A desire for something real, something not bought, may live in it.
boredom.practice: Recall an activity that once absorbed you with no use or purpose at all. What did you feel then?

joy.text: Joy is a gift, and you can trust it. In To Have or to Be?, Erich Fromm distinguished joy from pleasure. Pleasure, or thrill, in the having mode passes quickly and demands ever new stimuli — purchases, entertainment, impressions. Joy, for Fromm, accompanies living, productive activity: when you create, love, understand, take part. It is not a flash followed by a slump but more like a steady glow, a companion of being. Marcuse, for his part, insisted that the pursuit of happiness is a legitimate human demand, not a whim. From this point of view, your joy doesn’t need to be justified or “earned”: it tells you that right now you are truly alive and engaged.
joy.practice: Notice: is your joy right now connected with something you received, or with what you are doing and feeling? Just note it, without judging.

love.text: Love and tenderness are the heart of human life, and Fromm devoted a whole book to them. In The Art of Loving (1956), he argued against the idea that love is a pleasant feeling we happen to “fall into.” For Fromm, love is an art and an active power; it requires discipline, concentration, patience. He named its four foundations: care, responsibility, respect and knowledge of the other. Respect is the ability to see a person as they are and to want them to grow in their own way, not in the way that suits you. Fromm distinguished immature love, built on need, from mature love, in which two people unite while preserving themselves. Your tenderness is not weakness but the beginning of this art.
love.practice: Think of someone you love: how could you show them respect today — see them as they are?

quote.text: Immature love says: “I love you because I need you.” Mature love says: “I need you because I love you.”
quote.author: Erich Fromm

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling, full of life. The Frankfurt School didn’t write about gratitude as such, but from Fromm’s point of view one might say this. In The Art of Loving he observed that for the marketing character, giving means being deprived, so such a person gives only in exchange. For the “productive” character, however, giving is the highest expression of one’s own strength and vitality: in giving, a person experiences their own fullness. Gratitude is the mirror side of such giving: you receive something not as a transaction but as a sign of a living relationship. In a society where so much has been turned into calculation, the ability to give thanks without keeping score is a small expression of the mode of “being.” It connects you with others not through debt but through generosity.
gratitude.practice: Recall something you recently received that wasn’t in exchange for anything. Write down who it came from and what it meant to you.

hope.text: Hope is a very precious feeling, especially when it is hard to hold on to. In The Revolution of Hope (1968), Erich Fromm described it with subtlety. Hope is not passive waiting for someone to do everything for us, nor a frantic forcing of events that have not yet ripened. He compared it to a crouching tiger, which leaps only when the moment has come. Hope, for Fromm, is an inner readiness for what is not yet born. Marcuse, closing his most critical book, One-Dimensional Man, nevertheless left room for hope by quoting Walter Benjamin. From this point of view, hope doesn’t require certainty of a good outcome: it is a way of staying alive and open, even when the future is unclear.
hope.practice: Write down one small thing you are ready for, should it become possible. Not a plan — just readiness.

quote.text: Only for the sake of those without hope is hope given to us.
quote.author: Walter Benjamin
quote.source: essay “Goethe’s Elective Affinities”; Herbert Marcuse ends One-Dimensional Man (1964) with this line

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a warm, wistful longing for the past, and it is entirely natural. In Eros and Civilization, Marcuse gave memory special significance: the remembrance of happiness once lived, in his view, has a critical power — it reminds us that life can be better than it is now. From this point of view, nostalgia is not merely a retreat backward but a secret knowledge of what fullness can be. But in the spirit of Adorno and Horkheimer’s analysis of the “culture industry,” one can add a caution: the entertainment industry knows how to sell the past as a commodity — packaged, edited, painless. So it helps to distinguish your own memories from ready-made images of “the good old days.” Your nostalgia can hint at what you are missing now — and that is a valuable hint.
nostalgia.practice: Recall what you miss, and ask: what feeling from that time would I like to bring back into my life today?

craving.text: A sharp “I want it right now” can be almost unbearable, and there is nothing shameful in it. The Frankfurt School thought a great deal about how society handles our desires. Marcuse introduced the concept of “repressive desublimation”: the system readily offers quick, ready-made pleasures that relieve tension for a minute but leave the deeper need — for rest, closeness, meaning — unsatisfied. Adorno and Horkheimer wrote that consumer culture constantly promises satisfaction and constantly postpones it. From this point of view, a craving is not only your weakness: a real need often speaks through it, one that has been handed a substitute. A craving is like a wave: it rises, peaks and subsides. While it passes, you can ask yourself what this need is really asking for.
craving.practice: When a wave of craving comes, finish the sentence: “What I’m actually missing right now is…” — and simply read the answer, without deciding anything.

addiction.text: When life has long revolved around one thing, it is exhausting — and it is not a moral failure. In The Art of Loving (1956), Erich Fromm wrote that the deepest human need is to overcome one’s separateness, one’s aloneness. Among the ways people try to do this, he named “orgiastic states,” including alcohol and drugs, and stressed that these are understandable attempts, but afterward a person feels even more separate, and the circle closes. In The Sane Society (1955), Fromm added that much suffering is a response to a society in which it is hard to be alive and connected to others. From this point of view, addiction is a distorted search for connection, not a flaw of character. And so the way out, for Fromm, lies not in self-punishment but in a gradual return to living relationships.
addiction.practice: Write down the name of one person with whom you feel less separate. Sometimes such a person can be found in a mutual-help group too, where others know this cycle from the inside.

hangover.text: The morning after is heavy in both body and soul: anxiety, shame, fragments of last night. This is understandable, and you are not alone in it. In The Art of Loving, Fromm described how states of intoxication briefly give a sense of union and freedom, after which the opposite arrives — a sharp feeling of separateness, which is experienced as shame and anxiety. In Eros and Civilization (1955), Marcuse spoke of the “performance principle”: society expects us to be composed and efficient again by morning. Hence a double weight — you feel bad, and you’re not allowed to feel bad. From this point of view, one might say your “moral hangover” is partly fear of being judged by that principle. Today you can simply allow yourself to be a person who feels bad, without demanding an immediate account from yourself.
hangover.practice: Drink a glass of water slowly, noticing each sip. The question “what happened last night” can wait an hour — it isn’t going anywhere.

euphoria.text: A sudden high, when everything seems possible, is a vivid and valuable experience, and there’s no need to be ashamed of it. Adorno liked to repeat Stendhal’s words that beauty is “the promise of happiness.” In Eros and Civilization, Marcuse wrote that in moments of joy, in art and imagination, a person glimpses a different, freer life — one that everyday existence usually pushes aside. From this point of view, euphoria may be not an illusion but a brief flash of knowledge: yes, life can feel like this. The Frankfurt thinkers also soberly noted that society knows how to sell such flashes as commodities. So it is worth distinguishing where the high came from. But the image of what is possible that it showed you can be carefully kept.
euphoria.practice: Write in one sentence what exactly seems possible to you right now. Not as a plan, but as an image you want to remember.

crash.text: The drop after a high — a celebration, a success, a vivid evening — can be very noticeable, and it is not your fault. In Dialectic of Enlightenment (1947), Adorno and Horkheimer observed that entertainment in modern society is “the prolongation of work”: it exists to restore your strength for the next working day. The celebration is built into the schedule in advance, and a return to the usual rhythm inevitably follows. From this point of view, the comedown is not only chemistry or character but also a collision with the sharp contrast between a moment of freedom and an everyday life where there is little freedom. Understanding this means seeing that you are longing not for the high itself but for a life with more aliveness in it. That longing is not weakness but a sign that you need this aliveness.
crash.practice: Name one small living thing that was part of that high (laughter, a conversation, music), and think about whether you could let it into an ordinary Tuesday.

panic.text: A wave of panic is genuinely frightening: your heart pounds, your breathing falters, it feels as if something irreparable is about to happen. The Frankfurt School didn’t write about panic attacks, but something can be said in its spirit. In Eros and Civilization, Marcuse argued that society trains us to treat the body as an instrument that must work without fail. When the body suddenly slips out of control, it is especially frightening — after all, we were taught that control is the norm. From this point of view, instead of only fighting your body, you can for a minute take its side, as you would the side of a living creature that is scared. A wave like this usually rises, peaks, and within a few minutes begins to subside.
panic.practice: Place both feet on the floor and feel the support. Make your exhale longer than your inhale — slowly, several times, as if cooling hot tea.

dread.text: The question “what’s the point of it all?” and the sense of an abyss can hit with tremendous force, and this is an honest human experience. In The Jargon of Authenticity (1964), Adorno argued against philosophers who made the fear of death the central truth about the human being, almost heroizing it. He thought this lofty acceptance of finitude too easily turns into resignation to the way the world is arranged. In Eros and Civilization, Marcuse wrote that finitude is inevitable, but culture should not turn death into an ideal. Fromm contrasted “necrophilia” — an attraction to everything dead and mechanical — with “biophilia,” the love of what is alive. From this point of view, dread before the abyss is not a verdict but one side of a deep attachment to life. The Frankfurt thinkers looked for the answer to “what for?” in what is alive: in people, in work, in love.
dread.practice: Name three things that seem alive to you right now — a sound, a person, a plant. Linger on each for a few seconds.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives while you are somewhere you shouldn’t be is very common, and it isn’t only about you. Fromm described the “marketing orientation” of character: a person begins to perceive themselves as a commodity to be presented advantageously and constantly checks how others are “selling.” In One-Dimensional Man (1964), Marcuse showed that a vast choice of goods, experiences and entertainment does not in itself mean freedom: it may simply keep us in the race. From this point of view, the fear of missing out is largely a manufactured feeling: the system wins when we always feel that real life is somewhere else. This removes part of the guilt. And freedom, for Marcuse, begins where you can ask: do I actually need this?
fomo.practice: Choose one thing you are “missing out on” and ask: “Would I want this if nobody knew about it?”

quote.text: Free choice among a wide variety of goods and services does not signify freedom if these goods and services sustain social controls over a life of toil and fear.
quote.author: Herbert Marcuse

sleepless.text: Sleepless hours when your thoughts go round in circles can be very lonely and exhausting. The Frankfurt School didn’t write about insomnia directly, but from its point of view one might say that in the modern world the night, too, has fallen under the “performance principle” Marcuse spoke of. Sleep has become a resource to be properly replenished so that you work well tomorrow — and the anxiety “I won’t get enough sleep” itself keeps you awake. In his essay “Free Time” (1969), Adorno observed that even our rest is organized on the model of work. Perhaps your nighttime thoughts are what found no room during the day. From this point of view, you don’t have to demand efficiency from the night. It isn’t an exam. Even quiet rest without sleep is still rest.
sleepless.practice: If your thoughts won’t let go, write them on a sheet of paper by the bed, one line each, and tell yourself: “I’ll look at this in the morning.”

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply because it strikes at what is most vulnerable — trust. In Negative Dialectics (1966), Adorno wrote of “coldness” as the basic principle of life in a competitive society: everyone learns to protect their own interest first. Fromm described how relationships in such a society begin to resemble exchange — “you scratch my back, I’ll scratch yours.” From this point of view, betrayal is the moment when the logic of advantage or fear suddenly invades a relationship you thought was alive. This explains, but doesn’t excuse. And one more thing: the fact that you trusted is not naivety but that very capacity for living connection which the Frankfurt thinkers considered the most precious thing in a human being. You don’t have to give it up along with the loss.
betrayal.practice: Write: “I trusted because what mattered to me was…” — and finish with what exactly you value in relationships.

jealousy.text: Jealousy can be agonizing, and it often grows out of the fear of losing what is dearest. In To Have or to Be? (1976), Erich Fromm distinguished two ways of living: “having” and “being.” In the having mode, a loved one quietly becomes something you have and that can be taken away — and then any shadow of a threat triggers panic. In The Art of Loving (1956), Fromm described mature love as a paradox: two beings become one and yet remain two. From this point of view, jealousy is not proof of bad character but the voice of the anxiety of having, which everyone has. There’s no need to be ashamed of it. But you can notice where love says “you’re mine” and try to translate it into the language of being: “being with you is precious to me.”
jealousy.practice: Reframe one jealous thought from “I could lose you” into “what I treasure about what’s between us is…” and finish the sentence.

resentment.text: Long-held resentment is a heavy load, and if you carry it, you really were hurt once. In Escape from Freedom (1941), Erich Fromm wrote that destructive feelings — bitterness, hostility, the wish to pay back — grow where a person’s life is cramped and cannot unfold. The less room there is in a life for what is alive, the stronger the pull toward destruction. This is not a reproach to you, nor a demand that you forgive right away. It is a thought about where to look for relief: less in arguing with the person who hurt you inside your head, and more in widening your own life. Resentment keeps your gaze chained to the past. Fromm would suggest asking what else in your life is waiting for your attention and energy.
resentment.practice: Write down how much room the resentment takes up in your week, and one small thing that belongs only to your life, not to this story.

quote.text: Destructiveness is the outcome of unlived life.
quote.author: Erich Fromm

heartbreak.text: A breakup can feel as though a piece has been torn out of your life. In The Art of Loving (1956), Erich Fromm wrote that we often think of love as an “object”: the main thing is to find the right person, and to lose them is to lose love altogether. But for Fromm love is first of all a capacity, an activity, an “art” that lives within the person. He distinguished “falling in love” — the sudden collapse of the walls between people — from the ability to love, which stays with us even when a relationship has ended. From this point of view, you have lost a particular person and a shared life with them, and that is a real loss that needs to be mourned. But you haven’t lost the capacity to love: it is yours, and your pain is one of its signs.
heartbreak.practice: Write down what you learned about love in this relationship — one thing you now know how to do.

impostor.text: The fear of being found out any minute is familiar to a great many people — including those who are doing perfectly well. In Man for Himself (1947), Erich Fromm described the “marketing orientation”: in a society where everything is for sale, a person begins to feel like a commodity, and to experience their worth as a “price” set by others. Fromm quoted the title of Pirandello’s play: “I am as you desire me.” Then one’s sense of self becomes shaky: today I was valued, tomorrow I may be revalued. From this point of view, impostor syndrome is not your secret worthlessness but a natural consequence of a life in which worth is measured by demand. Fromm saw a footing in the “productive orientation” — in what you actually do and feel, not in someone else’s assessment.
impostor.practice: Write down one thing you did this week and describe it without judgment — just what you did and how.

self_hatred.text: When your inner voice is merciless, living with it is very hard, and you deserve gentleness — including your own. In Man for Himself (1947), Erich Fromm argued against the widespread idea that loving oneself is selfishness. He showed the opposite: respect and love for oneself and for others don’t compete but go together, and a person who can’t be kind to themselves has a hard time being kind to others. The inner critic, from Fromm’s point of view, often speaks with the voice of the “authoritarian conscience” — internalized demands of others — rather than your own “humanistic conscience,” which cares about your growth. Adorno added that real love is a place where you can be weak. Such a place can begin to be built inside yourself as well.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one sentence your inner critic says, and ask: “Whose voice is this?” Then write what someone who loves you would answer.

quote.text: You are loved only where you may show yourself weak without provoking strength.
quote.author: Theodor Adorno

helplessness.text: The feeling that you can’t change anything can be very heavy, and it deserves to be taken seriously. In Escape from Freedom (1941), Erich Fromm described how a person in the vast modern world — of markets, corporations, states — feels small and powerless. Adorno spoke of an “administered world,” where much is decided far away from us. From this point of view, your helplessness is partly a sober perception of reality, not your personal inadequacy. But in his essay “Resignation” (1969), Adorno insisted that even when action is almost impossible, the very capacity to think clearly and to disagree is not capitulation. You may not be able to change everything and still keep your own view, and the small acts that remain in your hands.
helplessness.practice: Divide a page into two columns: “beyond my power” and “a little within my power.” Write at least one small thing in the right-hand column.

procrastination.text: When you just can’t get started, it’s easy to accuse yourself of laziness. The Frankfurt School would suggest taking a wider view. In Eros and Civilization (1955), Marcuse wrote about the “performance principle”: our lives are more and more subordinated to the demand to be useful and efficient, and work is often experienced as something alien, imposed. Fromm spoke of alienation — a state in which a person doesn’t recognize themselves in what they do. From this point of view, one might say procrastination is sometimes a quiet resistance: part of you doesn’t want to give its energy to something in which it doesn’t feel itself. This isn’t a reason to drop everything but a reason to listen. Sometimes it’s enough to find even a tiny piece of the task that you do for yourself rather than for an evaluation.
procrastination.practice: Ask yourself: “What small piece of this task would I actually find interesting to do?” — and start with it for five minutes.

uprooted.text: When the ground has gone from under your feet — a move, emigration, the loss of a familiar world — it is a deep loss, even if the decision was right. Almost all the philosophers of the Frankfurt School — Adorno, Horkheimer, Marcuse, Fromm — were themselves émigrés, forced to leave Germany in the 1930s. Adorno wrote Minima Moralia (1951) in exile, subtitling it “Reflections from Damaged Life.” He acknowledged the pain of homelessness but also saw a special kind of knowledge in it: whoever has lost their home sees more clearly that the familiar order of things is not the only possible one. From this point of view, your uprootedness is not only a wound but also a new lens. It doesn’t cancel the longing, but it lets you not feel a stranger to everything in the world.
uprooted.practice: Write down one thing you now notice about the world or about your former life precisely because you ended up outside it.

quote.text: It is part of morality not to be at home in one’s home.
quote.author: Theodor Adorno

overload.text: The endless feed and information noise really are tiring — this is not your inability to “keep up.” In Dialectic of Enlightenment (1947), Adorno and Horkheimer described the “culture industry”: the production of entertainment and information according to the laws of the factory, where everything is standardized, fast and replaceable. They observed that this industry constantly promises satisfaction and constantly postpones it, which is why you keep wanting more. Marcuse added that a stream of ready-made impressions leaves less and less room for one’s own thought. From this point of view, overload is not a personal weakness but a natural reaction to an environment designed to hold your attention. Stepping away from part of the stream is not fleeing the world but reclaiming your right to think at your own pace.
overload.practice: Close the feed and sit for a minute with nothing new coming in. Notice one thought that arrived on its own, not from the screen.

unreality.text: The sense that everything around you, or you yourself, is somehow not quite real can be frightening and strange, and it deserves gentle care. The Frankfurt School didn’t describe this state as such, but from its point of view something important can be said. Adorno used the concept of “reification”: in a society where much is turned into commodity and function, living relationships begin to seem like things, and people like roles. Marcuse wrote of a “one-dimensional” world where everything is predictable and packaged in advance. In such a world, a sense of unreality may also be a signal of too little living contact, not only a glitch in perception. This doesn’t explain everything, but it lets you not be frightened of yourself: perhaps you are keenly feeling what many people have stopped noticing.
unreality.practice: Touch something with a distinct texture — fabric, wood, cold water — and name three sensations out loud.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious experience. In Aesthetic Theory (1970), Adorno gave great importance to the “shudder” — the instant when a person, faced with art or natural beauty, stops being closed in on themselves and feels something greater. He even wrote that the aesthetic relationship is ultimately defined by the capacity for such a shudder. For Adorno this experience is valuable because it cannot be fully bought, packaged or put to use. From this point of view, awe is one form of freedom: in these minutes you meet the world not as a consumer or a worker but as a living person. You can simply let it be.
awe.practice: Stay with what filled you with awe for one more minute, without taking a photo or telling anyone.

relief.text: Relief — when something heavy finally lets go — deserves to be noticed. In Eros and Civilization (1955), Marcuse distinguished the necessary repression without which shared life is impossible from “surplus repression” — excess strain demanded of us not by nature or by other people but by the way society is organized. From this point of view, relief is a moment when part of this excess load falls away, and for an instant you feel how much strength went into holding on. The experience also tells you what life could be like with a lighter load. You can simply enjoy it — and remember while you’re at it: this lightness is not an accidental luxury but something you truly need.
relief.practice: Take a deep exhale and notice where in your body it has become easier. Write down what exactly has let go.

calm.text: Calm is a state rarely found in the modern world, and it can be cherished. In one of the fragments of Minima Moralia (1951), Adorno argued against the ideal of unceasing activity and production. He invited us to imagine a different image of happiness — not endless growth and achievement, but simply existing, like an animal lying on the water and looking peacefully at the sky. Marcuse spoke of the “pacification of existence” as the goal of a free society: a life in which one doesn’t have to fight all the time. From this point of view, your calm is neither idleness nor wasted time but a touch of what, in the end, makes doing anything worthwhile at all. It doesn’t need to be justified by usefulness.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute looking out the window or at the sky, and do nothing — don’t even think about whether you are resting “correctly.”

quote.text: Rien faire comme une bête, lying on water and looking peacefully at the sky…
quote.author: Theodor Adorno

inspiration.text: Inspiration — the moment when you want to create and thought flows on its own — is one of the best sides of life. In To Have or to Be? (1976), Erich Fromm linked such moments to the mode of “being”: a person isn’t accumulating or appropriating but vividly, actively expressing themselves. He called this “productive” activity and distinguished it from mere busyness: you can be very busy and still create nothing of your own. In The Aesthetic Dimension (1977), Marcuse wrote that art and imagination can reveal another world that doesn’t coincide with what is. From this point of view, inspiration is not a whim but an expression of your capacity for freedom. It doesn’t have to be turned into a result right away — it is enough to give it room.
inspiration.practice: Write down what has just come to you, as it is — without editing, without judging, as a draft for yourself.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude — unexpected pleasure at someone else’s failure — is usually embarrassing to admit even to yourself. But many people know it, and the Frankfurt School helps us see its social side. In Dialectic of Enlightenment (1947), Adorno and Horkheimer wrote about the “culture industry”: in cartoons, Donald Duck gets his thrashing so that viewers grow used to the blows that come their own way. Where life is built on competition, someone else’s fall is felt for a moment as relief: so it isn’t me. From Fromm’s point of view, one might add that this is how the tension a competitive society builds up in everyone breaks through. Schadenfreude, then, is not your corruption but a trace of a system in which people are constantly compared. You can notice it and ask: what pressure of my own did it give me a break from?
schadenfreude.practice: Notice which area of your life feels most like a competition right now. Write down what you would want there if there were no comparison.

contempt.text: Contempt seems confident and cold, but tension often hides behind it. The Frankfurt School studied it seriously. Fromm described the “marketing orientation”: when a person’s worth is measured by success and demand, it’s easy to start dividing people into “winners” and “losers” — and to look down on the latter. In their study The Authoritarian Personality (1950), Adorno and his colleagues showed that contempt for the “weak” is often tied to fear of one’s own weakness: we reject in others what we fear in ourselves. From this point of view, contempt is not a trait of your character but a yardstick society slips to everyone. Instead of being ashamed of it, you can ask: by what scale am I judging this person right now — and would I myself measure up to that scale on a hard day?
contempt.practice: Write down exactly what you despise this person for. Then ask: who taught me that this deserves contempt?

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong bodily feeling: you want to turn away from people, a situation, sometimes from yourself. It doesn’t make you a bad person. In Minima Moralia (1951), Adorno didn’t hide his disgust at much of modern life — at falseness, huckstering, coldness — and treated it as a form of knowledge: sometimes disgust is the first to notice that something is wrong with the world. In The Heart of Man (1964), Fromm distinguished “biophilia” — love of everything living and growing — from an attraction to what is dead, mechanical, frozen. From this point of view, disgust can be a healthy reaction of a living person to what deadens. And then it matters to distinguish it from disgust at yourself, which is most often imposed from outside — by other people’s yardsticks and models. Disgust is worth listening to: what is it really pointing at?
disgust.practice: Finish the sentence: “It repels me because it is…” — and see what value your disgust is protecting: honesty, aliveness, dignity?

revenge.text: The wish for revenge usually grows out of a real hurt or injustice. The feeling is understandable, and it has its own dignity: you don’t accept that you can be treated this way. In The Heart of Man (1964), Erich Fromm described “revengeful violence” as a reaction to pain inflicted: it seeks not to protect but, as it were, to magically undo what happened. Fromm observed that vengefulness is stronger the fewer other supports a person has — a productive life, love, a sense of their own strength. Hence his thought: the antidote to revenge is not suppression but the widening of life. From this point of view, you can fully acknowledge the wish for revenge without acting on it, and ask: what part of my life has this wound now blocked from view — and how can I get it back?
revenge.practice: Write down one thing that makes you stronger and more alive, and give it a little time today. This doesn’t cancel the hurt, but it gives you back your life.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those closest to you — a partner, parents, children — can burn, and shame follows it. It is a very human feeling. Fromm called the family “the psychic agency of society”: through it the pressure, fatigue and anxieties of the wider world reach us, and at home they often spill out onto those nearest to us. In his work “Authority and the Family” (1936), Horkheimer showed how family relationships mirror the relations of power that exist in society. From this point of view, your anger may be not only about this person but also about the load you are both carrying. Fromm considered love not a feeling that either “is there or isn’t” but an activity of care, responsibility and respect. Anger doesn’t cancel it; but it matters not to let it spill out, and instead to translate it into words and requests.
anger_at_loved.practice: When the anger has subsided, ask yourself: “What is pressing on both of us?” Name one thing that depends neither on you nor on them.

quote.text: Love is the active concern for the life and the growth of that which we love.
quote.author: Erich Fromm

ambivalence.text: Loving and being unable to stand the same person is an exhausting but very human state. The Frankfurt School treated contradiction with care. In Negative Dialectics (1966), Adorno criticized “identity thinking” — the habit of forcing living reality under a single concept: “good” or “bad,” “I love” or “I don’t.” He believed truth often lives precisely in a contradiction that shouldn’t be hastily resolved. In The Art of Loving, Fromm wrote that mature love is a union in which each person keeps their separateness; and where two separate people meet, friction is inevitable. From this point of view, mixed feelings are not a sign that the relationship is false but a sign that you see the other person whole, not just the convenient part of them.
ambivalence.practice: Describe this person in three sentences, each containing both “I love” and “I can’t stand.” Notice how the picture changes when you don’t have to separate them.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, the death of a loved one, or long, draining care for someone who is ill often brings shame: how can I feel lighter? But relief and love can live side by side. In Man for Himself (1947), Fromm distinguished the “authoritarian conscience” — the internalized voice of external demands, which punishes any “improper” feeling — from the “humanistic conscience,” the voice of our own life, which cares that we stay alive and whole. From this point of view, shame about relief speaks in the authoritarian voice: “you must feel nothing but grief.” The humanistic conscience may say something else: you carried a heavy load for a long time, and breathing out is the natural right of a living person. This doesn’t cancel your love or diminish the loss.
guilty_relief.practice: Write down the sentence with which you reproach yourself. Ask: “Who is saying this — me, or some voice of duty?” — and write an answer in the voice of a caring friend.

indifference.text: Sometimes, where you “ought” to be moved — someone else’s misfortune, important news — there is only silence inside. It’s frightening, but it doesn’t mean you are heartless. In his lecture “Education after Auschwitz” (1966), Adorno spoke of “coldness” as a common trait of people in modern society: a life built on competition and the pursuit of self-interest teaches us to protect ourselves and wall ourselves off. He considered this coldness a problem not of individual character but of the whole social order. From this point of view, your indifference may be not emptiness but armor grown from overload. Adorno saw the first step not in shaming people but in coldness becoming aware of itself and its causes: understanding already makes it less all-powerful. Feelings can return once there is even a little safe space.
indifference.practice: Notice when you last felt something strongly, even over something small. Where was it, and what surrounded you then?

escape.text: The urge to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — and start over is familiar to very many people. It isn’t foolish: often it is the living part of a person speaking, the part that has run out of room. In Eros and Civilization (1955), Marcuse wrote about the “performance principle”: society demands above all that we function — work, conform, never stop. In The Sane Society (1955), Fromm used the word “alienation” for the state in which a person experiences their own life as someone else’s, as a set of roles. From this point of view, the urge to escape is not irresponsibility but the protest of what is alive against being turned into a function. It doesn’t call for immediate decisions at all. But it is worth listening to: it points to which parts of your life feel alien and which still feel like yours.
escape.practice: Divide a page into two columns: “Here I live” and “Here I function.” Fill in three items in each.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is “off limits” — unavailable, or “the wrong person” — can be confusing and frightening. In itself it doesn’t make you bad, and it decides nothing for you. In Eros and Civilization, Marcuse wrote of Eros as a life drive toward connection and fullness, one that is broader than the frames society assigns it. From this point of view, one might say that where life is tightly compressed by obligations, this striving can suddenly flare up in an unexpected direction. In The Art of Loving, Fromm distinguished “falling in love,” which seizes us, from love as an activity — care, responsibility, respect and knowledge of the other. Attraction to the unavailable can be looked at as a message: what aliveness, what recognition or freedom is your life missing right now? The answer to that question remains yours.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down who you become when you are near this person or thinking about them. Note where else in your life you would like that feeling.

social_anxiety.text: Shyness and fear of other people’s judgment make simple things hard: starting a conversation, speaking up, walking into a room. This is a very common experience. Fromm described the “marketing orientation”: in a society where everything is for sale, a person begins to treat themselves as a commodity whose value depends on how they are received. Then every appearance in public turns into a small exam in “marketability,” and it’s no wonder many people find it frightening. From this point of view, shyness is not only your personal trait but also a reaction to yardsticks society imposes on everyone. Fromm contrasted “having” and “being”: you don’t have to “have” a good impression; you can “be” in the conversation — take an interest in the other person, not only in how you look. This shift of attention brings noticeable relief.
social_anxiety.practice: In your next conversation, ask the other person one question whose answer genuinely interests you. Notice what happens to your fear while you listen.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is draining: it’s unclear what will happen, and there is nothing to lean on. The wish to know in advance is natural. In Dialectic of Enlightenment, Adorno and Horkheimer showed that all of modern civilization grew in large part out of this wish: to subdue nature, calculate everything, leave nothing unknown. But they also noticed that the pursuit of total control doesn’t free us from fear; it gives rise to new forms of it. In Escape from Freedom, Fromm wrote that insecurity is an inevitable side of freedom, and many people flee from it toward authorities and ready-made answers. From this point of view, the impossibility of knowing the future is not your personal failure but a shared condition of life from which no system is exempt. Bearing the unknown is also a form of freedom.
uncertainty.practice: Write down what you can’t know in advance, and separately, what you can do today, whatever the outcome.

quote.text: Man imagines himself free from fear when there is no longer anything unknown.
quote.author: Max Horkheimer, Theodor Adorno

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, results, news — stretches time out and keeps you from living: everything seems to be on pause. It’s hard. In his essay “Free Time” (1969), Adorno observed that in modern society the logic of work seeps even into leisure: time not occupied with something useful feels lost and empty. From this point of view, waiting is agonizing also because we are used to time being obliged to “deliver results.” In Eros and Civilization, Marcuse dreamed of time not subordinated to productivity alone — time for play, contemplation, unhurriedness. One might say: while there is no answer yet, your time still belongs to you. It doesn’t need to be “killed” or hurried; it can be lived — without pretending you don’t care, but also without handing your whole life over to waiting.
waiting.practice: For the next hour, choose one activity with no use at all — a walk, music, drawing — and let yourself spend that time just for its own sake.

regret.text: Regret about what you did or didn’t do can come back again and again. The feeling speaks of what mattered to you. Walter Benjamin, a friend and interlocutor of the Frankfurt School, described in his “Theses on the Philosophy of History” (1940) the “angel of history”: his face is turned toward the past; he would like to stay, awaken the dead and make whole what has been smashed, but a storm drives him forward. Benjamin believed the past is not definitively closed: remembrance can give it back its voice, and what was missed can still resonate in the present. From this point of view, regret is not useless self-torment but a memory of possibilities that haven’t entirely vanished. Some of them may come alive in a new form — in what you do now.
regret.practice: Write down what you regret, and next to it the value that lies behind it. Note one small action through which that value can live today.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person can be almost physical: you miss their voice, their presence, the familiar little things. This is the natural price of real connection. In The Art of Loving (1956), Fromm wrote that the deepest human need is to overcome one’s “separateness,” the aloneness of a separate being in the world. Love is the main answer to this need, which is why, when the beloved isn’t near, separateness is felt with new force. From this point of view, longing is not weakness but evidence that you managed to truly connect with another. Fromm considered love a capacity of the person themselves, not only a bond with one object — so it doesn’t vanish with their absence and can show itself in care, attention, creativity. You can live through longing without driving it away.
longing.practice: Do something today that this person loved, or that you did together — with them in mind. Let the longing take a form.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — for wars, injustice, grim news — can weigh on you so much that it’s hard to live an ordinary life. The feeling speaks of your capacity for compassion, and the Frankfurt School would take it seriously. Adorno, who lived through an age of catastrophes, insisted that suffering must be heard and expressed, not disguised. In his later years Horkheimer spoke of “the longing for the wholly Other” — the hope that injustice will not have the last word. From this point of view, your pain is neither naivety nor weakness but a sign that you refuse to accept suffering as normal. But it is impossible to carry it alone. Pain shared with others and turned into even a small action becomes more bearable.
world_pain.practice: Talk about what troubles you in the world with someone you trust. And then choose one small good deed close to home.

quote.text: Perennial suffering has as much right to expression as a tortured man has to scream.
quote.author: Theodor Adorno

rejection.text: Rejection hurts as though it wasn’t a request that was turned down but you as a whole. This pain is natural. In The Art of Loving, Fromm observed that most people experience love primarily as the problem of “being loved” — becoming attractive, earning being chosen — rather than as their own capacity to love. In a society arranged like a market, a refusal is easily experienced as “I wasn’t bought,” as if a price had been put on you. From this point of view, it is worth reminding yourself: you are not goods in a shop window, and someone’s refusal doesn’t determine your worth. It says that this particular meeting didn’t work out, not what you are worth. Your capacity to love, to be a friend, to take an interest in the world stays with you, whatever the other person answered.
rejection.practice: Write: “I wasn’t chosen for…, but I can still…” — and list three things.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can run very deep: it seems that without the other person there will be nothing to hold on to. This is understandable — connection with people is vital. In Escape from Freedom, Fromm described how modern people, freed from the old solid ties, were left alone with the anxiety of aloneness. In The Art of Loving he called one of the attempts to cope with it “symbiotic union”: dissolving into another so as never to be alone again. Fromm believed that such a bond, based on fear, makes us even more vulnerable. He described mature love as the union of two people, each of whom preserves their own integrity. From this point of view, working with the fear lies not in clinging more tightly to the other but in gradually strengthening your connection with yourself too: your interests, your supports, your life.
abandonment.practice: Write down three things that give you a sense of support and don’t depend on one person: an activity, a place, other people.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love wounds painfully: the feeling is there, but no answer comes. That doesn’t make it any less real. In The Art of Loving, Fromm stressed that love is first of all not what we receive but what we give: the capacity to care, to take an interest in the other, to rejoice in their life. He considered the capacity to love a strength of the one who loves, not a reward for reciprocity. From this point of view, your love is neither a mistake nor a defeat: it shows that you are capable of deep feeling. It hurts that right now it has found no answer, and that pain is worth living through without rushing yourself. But the capacity that showed itself in this love stays with you — and one day it may find another, mutual path.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love awakened in you: what qualities, what desires. This is yours, and it isn’t going anywhere.

quote.text: Love is an activity, not a passive affect; it is a “standing in,” not a “falling for.”
quote.author: Erich Fromm

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the hardest experiences: it feels as if your dignity has been taken from you, often in front of others. This pain is natural, and it says nothing about your weakness. Axel Honneth, a representative of the next generation of the Frankfurt School, showed in The Struggle for Recognition (1992) that for a healthy relationship to oneself a person needs recognition in three forms: love from those close to them, respect for their rights, and esteem for their contribution to the common good. Humiliation is a form of “misrecognition”: denying a person what is due to them as a person. That is why it wounds so deeply. But Honneth also saw in the experience of misrecognition a source of resistance: the pain of humiliation shows that you know what you deserve. From this point of view, your pain is the voice of your dignity.
humiliation.practice: Write down what respect you feel was taken from you. Then note the people or situations where you do have that respect.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body can be exhausting: the mirror turns into an exam. It is a very common feeling, and the Frankfurt School helps us see that it is not only personal. In Dialectic of Enlightenment, Adorno and Horkheimer wrote a note called “Interest in the Body”: civilization, in their view, relates to the body ambivalently — it both exalts and despises it, turning it into an object to be managed. The culture industry, Adorno would add, constantly supplies model bodies and faces by which we begin to measure ourselves. From this point of view, your shame is not only your problem but the imprint of yardsticks imposed on everyone. You can give your body back its place: not a commodity or a project, but a living self that feels, moves, rejoices.
body_shame.practice: For one minute, be in your body from the inside: warmth, breath, weight. Notice one pleasant sensation that has nothing to do with how you look.

illness.text: When your body lets you down — illness, pain, weakness — life changes, and irritation, fear and sadness are natural here. In Negative Dialectics, Adorno wrote about the “somatic moment” of thought: physical suffering tells cognition that suffering ought not to be, that things should be different. For him, bodily pain is not a trifle beside the “higher” questions but the place where honest philosophy begins. From Fromm’s point of view, one might add that a society living in the “having” mode teaches us to treat the body as property that is obliged to work properly — and then illness is experienced as a breakdown and a disgrace. But illness is not your fault and not a failure. Your pain has a right to be heard, and you have a right to care, not to reproaches from yourself.
illness.practice: Write down one sentence you would say to a friend who was ill — gentle, with no demands. Say it to yourself.

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a good and well-earned feeling; there’s no need to hide it. In Man for Himself (1947), Fromm described the “productive orientation” — a person’s capacity to use their powers: to create, to understand, to care. He distinguished it from the “marketing” orientation: the pride of the marketing person depends on how they are assessed, while the pride of the productive person comes from the activity itself, in which they expressed themselves. Fromm considered healthy self-love not selfishness but a condition for loving others. From this point of view, your pride is joy at having become a little more yourself. You can enjoy it without waiting for anyone else’s assessment, and notice which of your powers came alive in this work.
pride.practice: Write: “I’m proud that… and in doing it, what came out in me was…” The second part matters more than the first.

quote.text: Man’s main task in life is to give birth to himself, to become what he potentially is.
quote.author: Erich Fromm

melancholy.text: Bright sadness, melancholy, is a quiet feeling in which sorrow is mixed with tenderness toward the world. It doesn’t need fixing. The Frankfurt School knew this feeling intimately. In the dedication to Minima Moralia, Adorno called his book a “melancholy science” — an echo of Nietzsche’s The Gay Science: a thoughtful look at life, in his view, is inevitably tinged with sadness about what it could have been. In his book on German baroque drama (1928), Benjamin saw melancholy as a special form of attention: the melancholic lingers over things and notices in them what a hurried glance misses. From this point of view, bright sadness is not a malfunction but a way of seeing more deeply. You can live it like slow music, without letting it turn into despair.
melancholy.practice: Choose one object near you and look at it slowly for a minute, like Benjamin’s melancholic. Note something you hadn’t noticed before.
